subject: Cloud Computing
title: AWS Criticisms and Controversies
description: A short lesson to help you apply AWS Criticisms and Controversies.

hook.text: AWS hosts some of the most controversial platforms on the internet. Deciding who stays is political.

buildup.text: In 2021, AWS dropped Parler from its servers, reigniting debates about cloud provider power.

discovery.text: Critics argue that three companies controlling most cloud infrastructure is a dangerous concentration.

twist.text: AWS also faces antitrust scrutiny. Using its market data to compete with its own customers raises concern.

climax.text: Cloud dominance brings responsibility. AWS shapes what can exist online — and what can't.

punchline.text: AWS is infrastructure. But infrastructure is power.

quiz.question: What antitrust concern has been raised about AWS?
options: Using market data from its platform to compete with its own customers
Charging different prices in different countries

details.summary: AWS faces criticism for vendor lock-in through proprietary services, aggressive competition with its own customers by cloning popular tools, opaque pricing complexity, and its market power enabling potential anti-competitive behavior in the cloud industry.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding AWS's criticisms helps organizations make informed decisions about cloud strategy, dependency risk, and the trade-offs of building on the dominant platform.
takeaways: Proprietary services create deep vendor lock-in
AWS has been accused of cloning partner and customer products
Pricing complexity makes true cost comparison difficult

faq.question: How does AWS lock in customers?
faq.answer: Services like Aurora, DynamoDB, and Lambda use proprietary APIs that have no direct equivalent on other platforms. Data egress charges make it expensive to move data out. Years of accumulated infrastructure-as-code templates and team expertise create practical switching barriers.

faq.question: Has AWS really cloned customer products?
faq.answer: Several companies have accused AWS of observing which third-party services are popular on AWS Marketplace, then launching competing managed services. Notable examples include DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible), OpenSearch (Elasticsearch fork), and MemoryDB (Redis-compatible).
